                     PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR    §

AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF §
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY     §  PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST      §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION §
765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE      §              OF TEXAS
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET,      §
CONCHO, CORYELL, LAMPASAS,    §
LLANO, MASON, MCCULLOCH,      §
MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN     §
SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, §
AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES       §

          DONALD LEE JOINER AND ANITA M. JOINER EXHIBIT 1

     DONALD LEE JOINER’S DIRECT TESTIMONY OPPOSING LINK E4

        Donald Lee Joiner stipulates that this direct testimony can be treated by all

parties as if the answers were filed under oath and was originally filed as Item #

4176.

DIRECT TESTIMONY OF DONALD LEE JOINER ON BEHALF OF DONALD
LEE JOINER AND ANITA M. JOINER

PERSONAL INFORMATION

Q.      Please state your name and address.

A.      My name is Donald Lee Joiner. My mailing address is 5502 Pine Arbor Drive,

Houston, Texas 77066.




                               Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0001
 Q.    Are you the same Donald Lee Joiner who is the named intervenor in

the Joiner Motion to Intervene in this proceeding?

A.    Yes. The Joiner Motion to Intervene was filed as Item 1835 in PUC Docket No.

59475.

Q.    Please state your background.

A.    I am a retired Texas resident. Anita M. Joiner and I jointly own the Joiner

family farm in Williamson County, which has been in Anita’s family continuously

since the 1890s.

Q.    Are you testifying on behalf of yourself and Anita M. Joiner?

A.    Yes.

Q.    Is your property affected by the transmission line project proposed by

Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation?

A.    Yes. Anita and I own land identified in the Application as Tract 2665 and Tract

2680. Tract 2665 and Tract 2680 are adjoining parcels that, together, constitute a

single contiguous farm that has been operated as one farm for more than 120 years.

The proposed Link E4 passes directly through Tract 2665, follows the common border

between Tract 2665 and Tract 2680, and as a practical matter runs through the

middle of our family’s working farm.

      Two of our family homes flank the proposed Link E4 centerline. On the east

side of the proposed centerline, on a 2-acre parcel identified in the Application as

Tract 2680.1, sits the original Beyer/Joiner family home, which Anita’s grandfather




                              Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0002
 Maximilian Beyer built in 1900. We sold the 2-acre parcel and the original home to

our daughter Christy and her husband John Macon in 2003. The Beyer/Joiner family

home is identified in the Applicants’ materials as Habitable Structure 112 and,

according to Table 7-3 of Appendix E and the Macon direct testimony in this

proceeding, it sits 350 feet east of the Link E4 centerline. The Macons have separately

intervened, Item 314, and have filed direct testimony, Item 3650, opposing Link E4.

      On the west side of the proposed centerline sits a second family home that

Anita and I built on the farm in 2016 on the site of the original family home. The

second home sits approximately 600 feet west of the proposed Link E4 centerline. The

proposed centerline therefore runs between our 2016 home on the west and the

original Beyer family home (now owned by the Macons) on the east. The Beyer/Joiner

family home, which sits 350 feet east of the centerline, is one of the two habitable

structures within 500 feet of Link E4 reported by the Applicants. The 2016 Joiner

home at approximately 600 feet west of the centerline, is just outside the 500 foot

threshold but is the second occupied family residence flanking the proposed line.

Q.    Please describe the Joiners’ estate plan for the farm.

A.    Anita and I have five children. Our estate plan is to leave the Joiner family

farm to our five children. As part of that estate plan, the 2016 Joiner home that Anita

and I built on the west side of the proposed Link E4 centerline is designated to go to

our daughter, Kathleen Joiner. The Beyer/Joiner family home on the east side of the

proposed centerline is already in our daughter Christy’s family through the 2003 sale

of the 2-acre Tract 2680.1 to Christy and John Macon. The placement of Link E4




                               Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0003
 between these two family homes is therefore not just an impact on the current

owners; it is a permanent impact on the planned future ownership of the farm by the

next generation of our family.

Q.    What is the purpose of your testimony?

A.    The purpose of my testimony is to provide information and evidence supporting

rejection of any route that includes Link E4, and to identify Route 894 (which uses

the C4 to D12 corridor and stays in Bell County) as the route the Commission should

certify in the alternative. I also wish to address the harm that construction and

operation of a 765 kV transmission line would cause to two family homes on the same

farm, to our agricultural operations, to our groundwater and stock tanks, to the

wildlife and federally listed species habitat in this area, and to the heritage of land

that has been in our family for more than a century.

Q.    What routes do you oppose?

A.    I oppose Routes 376, 381, and 382 in their entirety because each of those routes

uses Link E4. I urge the Commission to reject those routes and to direct Oncor and

LCRA TSC to adopt an alternative route that avoids Link E4 and that maintains a

meaningful separation from all habitable structures, consistent with the prudent

avoidance principle in 16 Texas Administrative Code section 25.101(a)(6) and the

routing requirements in 16 Texas Administrative Code section 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv).

Q.    What route do you support?

A.    I support Route 894, which uses the C4 to D12 corridor and stays in Bell

County. Route 894 is the route the Applicants themselves have identified as best




                                 Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0004
 addressing PURA and the Commission’s Substantive Rules. I also support any other

route that uses the C4 to D12 corridor and avoids Link E4.

Q.    Have you ever testified at the Public Utility Commission of Texas

before?

A.    This is my first time testifying before the Public Utility Commission of Texas.

Q.    Was this material prepared by you or under your supervision?

A.    Yes.

DESCRIPTION AND LOCATION OF THE PROPERTY

Q.    Please provide a brief description of the property.

A.    The Joiner family farm consists of Tract 2665 and Tract 2680 as identified in

the Application materials. Tract 2665 and Tract 2680 are adjoining parcels that we

farm together as a single contiguous unit. The farm is in Williamson County, Texas,

in the eastern portion of the study area for the Bell County East to Big Hill 765 kV

transmission line project. The farm includes cultivated crop fields, native pasture

used for cattle grazing, stock tanks built over the past century, and habitat that

supports diverse wildlife. The surrounding landscape is mainly rural and agricultural

and lies within the area covered by the Williamson County Conservation

Foundation’s habitat conservation work.

      Carved out of Tract 2680 is a 2-acre parcel, Tract 2680.1, on which the

Beyer/Joiner family home sits. We sold the 2-acre parcel and the original home to our

daughter Christy and her husband John Macon in 2003. In 2016, Anita and I built a

second family home on the Joiner farm. The 2016 Joiner home is on the west side of




                              Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0005
 the proposed Link E4 centerline and is designated in our estate plan to pass to our

daughter Kathleen Joiner. The proposed Link E4 centerline therefore runs between

the Beyer/Joiner family home (now owned by the Macons, on the east) and the 2016

Joiner home (designated to go to Kathleen, on the west).

Q.       Please give a brief history of the property and your association with

it.

A.       The land has been in Anita’s family in continuous ownership and active use

since the 1890s. The original family home was built in 1900 by Anita’s grandfather

Maximilian Beyer. Anita’s father grew up in that house, Anita herself grew up in that

house, and our daughter Christy and her husband John Macon now live in that house.

The land and the home represent more than a century of stewardship, labor, and

heritage.

         Between 1999 and May 2025, record title to Tract 2665 and Tract 2680 was

held by the 1999 Joiner Family Trust, a revocable trust of which Anita and I were the

beneficiaries. In May 2025, the Trust was revoked, and ownership of Tract 2665 and

Tract 2680 was returned to Anita and me in our individual capacities. The 1999

Joiner Family Trust was the addressee on the direct landowner notice provided by

the Applicants. We are therefore included on the Landowner Mailing List filed as

part of the Application and received the direct notice required by the Commission’s

rules.

Q.       Please describe how the property is used today and how this

transmission line may affect that use.




                               Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0006
 A.    The Joiner family farm is in active agricultural use. We have cultivated crop

fields that produce hay and seasonal row crops that provide income and feed for the

operation. We have native pasture used for cattle grazing. We have stock tanks that

water the cattle. The land supports white-tailed deer, migratory birds, and other

native wildlife. The Beyer/Joiner family home on Tract 2680.1 is the family residence

of Christy and John Macon. The 2016 Joiner home that Anita and I built on the west

side of the proposed Link E4 centerline is part of the family’s planned generational

succession on the farm and is designated for our daughter Kathleen Joiner.

      The proposed Link E4, if constructed as proposed, would permanently damage

the property in the following ways. First, the towers and conductors would sit

between the Beyer/Joiner family home (350 feet east of the centerline) and the 2016

Joiner home (approximately 600 feet west of the centerline), placing the Macon family

home within the 500 foot prudent avoidance band identified in 16 Texas

Administrative Code section 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv) and placing the 2016 Joiner home

just outside that band on the opposite side of the centerline. Second, the 200-foot right

of way corridor would bisect the working farm by following the common boundary line

between Tract 2665 and Tract 2680, which means the corridor would pass straight

through the heart of our farming operations rather than skirting the perimeter.

Third, the construction process would disrupt crop production for at least one full

growing season and would require pasture closure during foundation drilling and

tower assembly. Fourth, the lattice tower locations within the cropland would create

permanent obstacles for farm equipment and recreational vehicles.




                                Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0007
 Q.     What is the proposed distance between Link E4 and the structures on

the property?

A.     The centerline of Link E4 is proposed approximately 350 feet east of the

Beyer/Joiner family home (Habitable Structure 112) and approximately 280 feet east

of the Macon guest apartment and workshop. The 2016 Joiner home that Anita and

I built sits approximately 600 feet west of the centerline. With a 200-foot right of way,

the edge of the right of way will be 250 feet from the Beyer/Joiner family home and

approximately 500 feet from the 2016 Joiner home. Link E4 follows the common

boundary between Tract 2665 and Tract 2680, an internal line that runs through the

middle of our farming operations.

FINANCIAL AND PROPERTY VALUE IMPACTS

Q.     What do you think the financial risks will be to the Joiner family?

A.     The financial risks to our family are severe and likely permanent. The farm is

the principal heritage asset of our family and the asset around which our estate plan

for our five children is built. A 200-foot right of way for a 765 kV line, with steel lattice

towers up to 198 feet tall, will permanently devalue the farm, both family homes

flanking the centerline, and the residual agricultural value of the surrounding tracts.

Q.     Will the property value impact be limited to the homes?

A.     No. The 200-foot corridor on Tract 2665 and along the Tract 2665/2680

boundary will affect the marketability and value of the entire farm. Tower footprints

remove productive acres from cultivation and grazing. Buyers discount land

burdened by transmission easements. The visual and audible presence of the line




                                 Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0008
 diminishes the rural character that drives Williamson County land prices. A 200-foot

right of way through the middle of the farm eliminates any reasonable expectation

that the farm will retain its current market or heritage value for any of our five

children.

HEALTH RISKS

Q.    What do you think are the health risks?

A.    Anita and I, and our extended family, are concerned about the health effects of

an energized 765 kV transmission line passing between two family homes on the

same farm.

SAFETY RISKS

Q.    What do you see as safety risks?

A.    The safety risks of the proposed Link E4 are substantial. First, the proximity

of a 765 kV line to occupied structures creates a risk of arc flash, stray voltage, and

induced current on nearby metal structures such as fences, water troughs,

outbuildings, and farm equipment. Second, Williamson County experiences

significant severe weather events including tornadoes and high winds. A tower

collapse or conductor break from a severe weather event between the two family

homes is a real risk. Third, the construction process itself, including heavy

equipment, auger drilling for tower foundations, concrete pouring, and conductor

stringing, creates immediate physical danger near the family homes and farm

operations. Fourth, the towers themselves are obstacles that present collision risks

to farm equipment, and to vehicles used in the daily operation of the farm.




                               Joiner Exhibit 1 – 0009
 ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACTS AND RISKS

Q.     What do you think will be the environmental impacts and risks?

A.     The environmental impacts are multifold. First, soil erosion is a significant

risk during and after right of way clearing on the farm. Clearing and grading along a

200-foot right of way through Tract 2665 and along the Tract 2665 and Tract 2680

boundary would expose soils to wind and water erosion. Second, ongoing herbicide

application under the conductors poses risks of drift and soil absorption into adjacent

crop fields, pasture, livestock, and native vegetation. Third, Link E4 enters

Williamson County, where the proposed corridor would pass over the Edwards

Aquifer.

Q.     What do you think will be the risks to your stock tanks and

groundwater?

A.     The Joiner family farm relies on stock tanks built over the past century to

water cattle. A water well on the property is used for domestic water and irrigation.

Runoff of herbicides used to maintain vegetation on the right of way could endanger

the safety of these water sources. Clearing of vegetation along the right of way also

increases surface runoff velocity and erosion, which can transport sediment, debris,

and agricultural chemicals into the stock tanks, reducing their capacity and water

quality for cattle.

       The Edwards Aquifer adds another concern. Tower foundation drilling

penetrates the soil and substrate above the karst formation. Even with best




                              Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00010
 management practices, that work risks introducing surface contaminants into a

critical groundwater resource.

RISKS TO WILDLIFE AND FEDERALLY LISTED SPECIES

Q.    What do you think will be the risks to wildlife and federally listed

species?

A.    The risks to wildlife on the family farm and the surrounding area are

significant. The Applicants’ Environmental Assessment identifies Williamson County

as habitat for several federally and state-listed species.

RISKS TO AGRICULTURAL ACTIVITIES

Q.    What do you think will be the risks to your agricultural activities and

animals?

A.    The risks to the family cattle operation and crop production are direct and

severe. The proposed Link E4 cuts straight through the heart of our farming

operations because it follows the internal common boundary between Tract 2665 and

Tract 2680. The specific risks include the following.

      First, stray voltage and induced EMF: high-voltage transmission lines are

known to cause stray voltage on metal fences, water troughs, and farm equipment,

which disrupts cattle behavior, reduces feed intake, and causes cattle to avoid water

sources and feeding areas near the right of way.

      Second, right of way fragmentation: a 200-foot corridor down the internal

boundary line of the farm bisects the working operation. The towers, which the EA

describes as steel lattice structures up to 198 feet tall in EA Section 1.3.1 at page 1-




                               Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00011
 6, will provide additional obstacles that have to be navigated during row crop

operations and during cattle movement across the right of way.

      Third, crop damage from construction: tower foundation construction involves

drilling and pouring four concrete piers per tower to significant depths, which will

permanently disturb multiple locations in the cropland.

      Fourth, herbicide contamination: as discussed above, herbicide application for

right of way vegetation management poses a risk of crop contamination, pasture

damage, and stock tank contamination from herbicide runoff.

      Fifth, construction noise and traffic: cattle are sensitive to sudden noise and

vibration, and the construction process can cause weight loss, injury from panicked

movement, and reproductive disruption during the active construction phase.

ENJOYMENT, FUTURE USE, AND COMMUNITY VALUES

Q.    How would the transmission line affect your family’s enjoyment of the

property?

A.    The proposed Link E4 would devastate our family’s enjoyment of this property.

The Beyer/Joiner family home and the 2016 Joiner home, both of which sit on land

that has been in Anita’s family for over 130 years, are situated in a rural Williamson

County setting that the family has always prized for its natural beauty, quiet, clear

skies, and open views. The installation of steel lattice towers up to 198 feet tall

between the two family homes would permanently eliminate those qualities. The

visual impact would be immediate and overwhelming from either home. The audible




                              Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00012
 presence of a 765 kV line, which generates persistent corona buzzing and crackling

especially in wet or humid weather, would be present at all hours.

Q.     Will the proposed transmission line affect any planned future use on

your land?

A.     Yes. Anita and I have five children, and our estate plan is to leave the Joiner

family farm to them. The 2016 Joiner home on the west side of the proposed Link E4

centerline is designated specifically to pass to our daughter Kathleen Joiner. The

Beyer/Joiner family home on the east side of the proposed centerline is already in our

daughter Christy’s family. The presence of a 765 kV transmission line between those

two homes, and through the middle of the farm, eliminates the residential use value

of both homesteads and substantially reduces the agricultural and heritage value of

the farm for all five of our children.

Q.     How would this transmission line affect your rural community values?

A.     Williamson County’s rural western areas retain the agricultural heritage and

open-land character that define this community’s values. Our extended family has

been part of this community since the early 1890s, contributing to its ranching and

farming tradition, its rural landscape, and the conservation of its natural resources.

The land use in the area is predominantly agricultural. The construction of a 765 kV

transmission line through active farm operations fragments the landscape, disrupts

agricultural practices, reduces property values for all neighboring landowners, and

changes the visual and economic character of the community. This is not an isolated




                                Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00013
 concern; it is shared with the Macons, with our farming neighbors, and with the rural

community of western Williamson County.

Q.    How will this transmission line affect the aesthetic value of your

property?

A.    The aesthetic impact of Link E4 on our property would be total and permanent.

The Application materials and the EA acknowledge that aesthetic impacts exist when

structures alter the character of the existing visual environment exposing residents

to the views of the structures and wires. For our property specifically, where towers

would sit between the two family homes, the alteration of the existing visual

environment would mean complete destruction of the natural scenic character of both

homes and their surroundings. Tower lights on structures would introduce

permanent light pollution into a previously dark rural setting. No amount of

landscaping or vegetation management can screen a 198-foot steel lattice tower at

this distance.

ROUTING, SERVICE, AND COST

Q.    Does the proposed transmission line parallel any existing rights of

way on your property?

A.    To the best of my understanding, no. According to Table 7-3 of Appendix E at

page 3, Link E4 runs zero feet parallel to existing electric transmission lines, zero

feet parallel to railroads, zero feet parallel to public roads or highways, and zero feet

parallel to pipelines. The only parallelism credited in Table 7-3 is 5,502 feet parallel

to apparent property boundaries, which Oncor admits is based on tax parcel boundary




                               Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00014
 data. In our case, the parallel-to-property-boundaries figure for Link E4 reflects the

internal line that splits the Joiner family farm, not the outer perimeter of the

contiguous landowner holdings. We support routing that follows existing

transmission line corridors, roadways, or other compatible features in lieu of cutting

a new right of way through a working farm and between two century-old or near-

century-old family homes.

FURTHER MATTERS FOR THE COMMISSION

Q.    Is there anything else you would like to have considered in this

proceeding?

A.    Yes. I wish to emphasize several overarching points for the Commission’s

consideration.

      First, the proposed Link E4 would not just sit near a single home. It would sit

between two family homes on the same heritage farm. The Beyer/Joiner family home,

built in 1900 and now owned by our daughter Christy and her husband John Macon,

sits 350 feet east of the proposed centerline. The 2016 Joiner home, designated in our

estate plan to pass to our daughter Kathleen Joiner, sits approximately 600 feet west

of the proposed centerline. The Beyer/Joiner family home is one of the two habitable

structures within 500 feet of Link E4 reported in Table 7-3 of Appendix E. The 2016

Joiner home, at approximately 600 feet west of the centerline, is just outside the 500

foot threshold but flanks the line on the opposite side from the Macon home. The

Applicants’ own materials show that prior versions of route links were modified




                              Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00015
 specifically to increase distance from habitable structures and to follow road and

property line corridors.

      Second, the Joiner family farm is not just property. It is more than 130 years

of history, labor, and heritage. The Beyer/Joiner family home was built in 1900 by

Anita’s grandfather Maximilian Beyer. Anita’s father grew up in the house, Anita

grew up in the house, and our daughter Christy and her husband John Macon now

live in the house. Anita and I built the 2016 Joiner home on the west side of the

proposed centerline as part of our generational succession plan. Our five children are

the planned future owners of this farm. Century-old family farm operations like ours

represent exactly the kind of historic and cultural resource that the routing process

should work to protect.

      Third, the Williamson County portion of the study area is environmentally

sensitive in ways the Applicants may have underweighted. The North Williamson

County Karst Fauna Region, the Edwards Aquifer Northern Segment, the federally

listed Salado Springs Salamander, the federally endangered Bone Cave Harvestman

and Coffin Cave Mold Beetle, and the federally endangered Golden-cheeked Warbler

habitat all argue for a routing solution that minimizes disturbance to this area, not

one that runs a 200-foot right of way through it.

      Fourth, the cost estimates in the record are conceptual. The estimated cost of

$25,797,000 for Link E4 does not include the federal karst zone Pre Construction

Notification work, the TCEQ Edwards Aquifer Protection Program compliance, the

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service coordination on the Salado Springs Salamander




                              Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00016
 critical habitat, the Bone Cave Harvestman and Coffin Cave Mold Beetle in the North

Williamson County KFR, the Golden-cheeked Warbler in the eastern study area, or

any archaeological or historic resource survey work along the 5,092 feet of E4 that

runs through high archaeological or historical site potential. These site-specific costs

all attach to Link E4 specifically because of its Williamson County entry. Indeed, the

E4 routes are all significantly longer than the recommended route. Each extra mile

is extra cost to build and maintain the line.

        Fifth, if the Bell County East to Big Hill 765 kV transmission line project is

approved, I respectfully request that the Commission certify Route 894 or another

route that uses the C4 to D12 corridor and avoids Link E4.

Q.      Does that conclude your testimony?

A.      Yes, at present it does, but I reserve the right to amend or supplement my

testimony. I respectfully request that the Commission give full and serious

consideration to the harms I have described, and that it require the Applicants to

develop and adopt an alternative route for the eastern end of the project that does not

place a 765 kV transmission line between two family homes on the same heritage

farm.




                               Joiner Exhibit 1 – 00017
